From reach to recurring

Revenue · Media

In short: reach is rented, recurring is owned. The move is from traffic-dependent revenue to products people pay for repeatedly, measured by conversion, churn, revenue per subscriber and platform independence.

Key points

  • Programmatic ads, evergreen affiliate links and traffic-based sponsor pricing are exposed when assistants answer without sending visitors.
  • Put analysis, access, data or community behind the paywall, not the news everyone has.
  • Price sponsorship per campaign against a named audience and prove it with response, not impressions.
  • Keep search-dependent affiliate revenue out of the core forecast until owned channels drive it.
  • Report the share of revenue not dependent on platforms first, every month.

The answer-engine problem

For twenty years the deal was simple. You published, search engines sent people, and you sold the attention. That deal is being rewritten without you.

AI assistants now answer directly. A reader asks a question, gets a synthesised answer, and never visits the page that supplied the facts. The attention still exists. It just stops at the assistant.

Any media business whose revenue depends on search referrals is exposed. Programmatic advertising, affiliate links on evergreen pages, and traffic-based sponsor pricing all sit in the path.

Three responses hold up.

Owned channels. Email, membership, apps and communities are relationships no intermediary can intercept. Part 26 covered why owned beats rented. This is the practical reason.

Be the source. Assistants cite original reporting, proprietary data, and clear expert positions. They do not cite the fourth rewrite of a press release. Being cited builds brand and sends some traffic, but the real value is authority that converts to paid.

Products that do not need traffic. Everything in the rest of this part.

Subscriptions and memberships

The paid relationship is the core of a recurring media business. It is also where most founders under-invest, because free growth feels better than paid conversion.

Three decisions drive it. What is behind the wall, how you ask, and what happens after someone pays.

Behind the wall should sit the thing your point of view produces: analysis, access, data, or community. Not the news everyone has. The ask should be specific and tied to a moment of value, not a generic banner. After payment, onboarding and the first renewal matter more than acquisition.

Membership adds a second layer: belonging, access to people, and influence over what gets made. Part 5 covers community as a job. Membership is where that job gets paid for.

B2B data, research and sponsorship on quality

Business audiences pay for things that reduce their risk or save them time. A publisher covering a sector sits on exactly that material.

Data products: benchmarks, pricing, deal flow, rankings, directories. Research products: reports, briefings, surveys, advisory calls. Both sell on annual contracts with renewal, and both are priced on usefulness, not on audience size.

Sponsorship changes with the same logic. Stop selling CPM. Sell access to a defined audience with a defined behaviour, and price on that.

Old sponsorship Quality sponsorship
Priced per thousand impressions Priced per campaign against a named audience
Proof is delivery numbers Proof is response, leads or renewal
Sold to media buyers Sold to marketing and sales leaders
Renewal depends on traffic Renewal depends on results

A sponsor who renews is worth more than three who try once. Build the sales process around renewal from the first conversation.

Affiliate, commerce and events

Affiliate and commerce work when they match the point of view and are disclosed clearly. Recommending what you would recommend anyway, with a visible note that you earn on it, keeps trust intact. Hiding it loses the trust and the revenue together.

Keep affiliate revenue out of the core forecast if it depends on search traffic. It belongs in the exposed column until it is driven by owned channels.

Events can be the highest-margin line or the most expensive mistake. The difference is the model. Small, repeated, sponsor-backed gatherings with ticketed access tend to work. One large annual event with a cost base set before sponsors sign tends not to.

Part 8 covers distribution when platforms are closed. Events are distribution and revenue in one, which is why they deserve a proper plan rather than an experiment.

Metrics for the move

Part 9 says stop reporting reach. Media needs to replace it with a short set of numbers that show the move from traffic to recurring.

  • Paid conversion: share of free audience that becomes paying over a defined period.
  • Churn: share of paying relationships lost per period, by cohort.
  • Revenue per subscriber: total recurring revenue divided by paying relationships.
  • Sponsor renewal rate: share of sponsors who buy again.
  • Share of revenue not dependent on platforms: the number that tells you how exposed you are.

Report these monthly. Put the last one at the top. I treat it as the single figure that tells a media founder whether the business is theirs or the platform's.

Part 10 covers building it to run without you. In media that means systems for renewal, sponsor reporting and product delivery that do not route through the founder's inbox.

The checklist

  • [ ] Traffic-dependent revenue identified and labelled as exposed
  • [ ] Owned channel growth tracked separately from platform growth
  • [ ] Paid product defined around the point of view, not around general news
  • [ ] Sponsorship priced on audience definition and results, not CPM
  • [ ] Affiliate and commerce disclosed, and excluded from the core forecast if traffic-driven
  • [ ] Five recurring metrics reported monthly, platform independence first

Common questions

How do AI answer engines affect publisher revenue?

Assistants answer directly, so readers often never visit the page that supplied the facts. Revenue that depends on search referrals, such as programmatic ads, evergreen affiliate links and traffic-priced sponsorships, is exposed.

What metrics should a media business track instead of reach?

Paid conversion, churn by cohort, revenue per subscriber, sponsor renewal rate and the share of revenue not dependent on platforms, reported monthly with the last one first.

How should a niche publisher price sponsorships?

Per campaign against a named audience, proven by response, leads or renewal rather than impressions, and sold to marketing and sales leaders rather than media buyers.

What kind of events work for media companies?

Small, repeated, sponsor-backed gatherings with ticketed access tend to work. One large annual event with costs set before sponsors sign tends not to.
